A battery that keeps going flat may be fine and simply not being charged, or something may be draining it while the car is parked. A load test of the battery and a check of the alternator output tell you which.
A clunk when you move the selector can be worn engine or gearbox mounts as well as an internal fault. A workshop can tell the two apart quickly.

A fault code says which reading was out of range, not which part failed. A "lean mixture" code, for example, can come from an air leak, a sensor, a weak fuel pump or a clogged injector. Testing the suspect parts is what separates a correct repair from replacing parts on a guess.
A fault code tells you where to start looking, not what to replace. We trace faults to their cause so you only pay for the repair you need.

A flashing light typically means the engine is misfiring. Unburnt fuel can overheat and damage the catalytic converter, which is an expensive part. Ease off, avoid hard acceleration, and get the car checked as soon as possible.
A flat battery is not always a bad battery. We test the battery under load, check the alternator's charging output, and look for anything draining the battery while the car is parked.

A leaking gasket, a stretched timing chain or a failed head gasket can often be fixed without a full rebuild. A full overhaul makes sense when wear is spread across the engine, or when the engine is already apart and the extra work costs little more.
A musty smell usually comes from a dirty cabin filter or mould on the evaporator. Replacing the filter and cleaning the system usually cures it.

A proper service also covers filters, brake fluid, coolant, spark plugs and a safety inspection at the intervals your maker sets. Keep the receipts: a complete service history helps when you sell the car.
A pulsing pedal or shaking steering wheel under braking usually comes from uneven disc thickness. Discs are measured and replaced if they are below the minimum thickness stamped on them.

A routine service starts with the engine oil and oil filter, then works through the items your car maker lists for that interval: air filter, cabin filter, spark plugs, brake fluid, coolant, gearbox oil where the maker specifies it, and a check of belts, hoses, tyres, brakes, suspension, lights and battery.
A seized caliper or slide pin, a collapsed brake hose or contaminated pads can make one side brake harder than the other. This also wears tyres unevenly.

A steady check engine light means the engine computer has stored a fault and the car should be checked soon. A flashing light usually means a severe misfire that can damage the catalytic converter, so drive gently and get the car to a workshop straight away.

A steady light means a fault has been stored; get it checked soon. A flashing light usually means the engine is misfiring badly enough to damage the catalytic converter, so reduce speed, avoid hard acceleration and have the car looked at straight away.

A thump between gears, or a pause before the next gear engages, often comes from old fluid, a sticking solenoid in the valve body, or adaptation values that need resetting. Software and fluid issues are the cheaper end of gearbox repair, which is why it pays to check early.
